cards: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman whose victory in civil war made him dictator, before his assassination in 44 BCE.
Strabo was a Greek geographer and historian from Amaseia in Pontus, active under Augustus and Tiberius.
c. 64 BCE – c. 24 CE · Ancient Near East
Livy (Titus Livius) was a Roman historian from Patavium (Padua) who wrote Ab Urbe Condita, a history of Rome from its foundation in 142 books, of which 35 survive.
Lucius Cornelius Sulla was a Roman general and statesman.
Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Empire, reigning from 51 to 30 BCE.
Cicero (Marcus Tullius Cicero) was a Roman statesman, lawyer, orator and philosopher, the greatest master of Latin prose.
Diodorus Siculus was a Greek historian from Agyrium in Sicily who wrote the Bibliotheca historica, a universal history in forty books from mythical times to about 60 BCE.
Vercingetorix was a chief of the Arverni who in 52 BCE united most of the Gauls in revolt against Julius Caesar.
Gaius Valerius Catullus was a Roman poet from Verona, active in the late Republic.
Juba I was king of Numidia from about 60 to 46 BCE.
Ovid was a Roman poet, born at Sulmo in the land of the Paeligni in 43 BCE, the author of the Metamorphoses, the Art of Love and the Fasti, a poem on the Roman calendar and its festivals.
Cassivellaunus was a British war leader who led the resistance to Julius Caesar's second invasion of Britain in 54 BCE.
Nero Claudius Drusus, known as Drusus the Elder, was a Roman general, stepson of the emperor Augustus and younger brother of Tiberius.
Virgil was a Roman poet of the Augustan age, author of the Eclogues, the Georgics and the Aeneid, the epic of Rome's legendary Trojan origins.
Burebista was a king of the Getae and Dacians who, from about 82 BCE, united their tribes into a powerful kingdom, aided by the high priest Deceneus.
Juba II was the son of King Juba I of Numidia, raised in Rome after his father's defeat by Julius Caesar.
c. 48 BCE–23 CE · Egypt & North Africa
Sallust (Gaius Sallustius Crispus) was a Roman politician and historian.
Lucretius, in full Titus Lucretius Carus, was a Roman poet and philosopher of the first century BCE.
Pharnaces II was a son of Mithridates VI of Pontus.
Ariovistus was a Germanic leader of the Suebi who crossed the Rhine into Gaul around 70 BCE as an ally of the Sequani and Arverni against the Aedui.
Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator who led the largest slave revolt against the Roman Republic, the Third Servile War of 73–71 BCE.
Wang Mang was a Han court official and relative of the empress dowager who seized the throne in 9 CE and founded the Xin dynasty.
c. 45 BCE–23 CE · Central & East Asia
Herod the Great was an Idumaean named king of Judea by the Roman Senate in 40 BCE, who took Jerusalem from the last Hasmonean king in 37 BCE.
Horace, Quintus Horatius Flaccus, was a leading Roman poet of the age of Augustus.
Huhanye was a chanyu, or supreme ruler, of the Southern Xiongnu during the succession conflicts of the mid-first century BCE.
Maues was the first major Indo-Scythian king in India, ruling in the early 1st century BCE.
r. c. 85–60 BCE · Central & East Asia
Amanirenas was a ruling queen, or kandake, of the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë.
fl. c. 40–10 BCE · Egypt & North Africa
Amanishakheto was a ruling queen, or kandake, of the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë in the late 1st century BCE.
fl. late 1st century BCE · Egypt & North Africa
Caesarion, formally Ptolemy XV, was the son of Cleopatra VII and, by her account, of Julius Caesar.
Gaius Cornelius Gallus was a Roman poet and soldier who became the first prefect of Egypt after its annexation in 30 BCE.
Hermaeus was one of the last Indo-Greek kings, ruling in the Paropamisadae around the Kabul valley in the early 1st century BCE.
fl. c. 90–70 BCE · Central & East Asia
Hiarbas was a king of Numidia in the early first century BCE, installed after the expulsion of Hiempsal II with the backing of the Marian faction in Rome's civil war.
Posidonius was a Greek Stoic philosopher, historian and scientist from Apamea in Syria who settled on Rhodes, where he ran a famous school and held public office.
Ptolemy XII Auletes was king of Ptolemaic Egypt from 80 to 58 BCE and again from 55 to 51 BCE, and father of Cleopatra VII.
Publius Canidius Crassus was a Roman general and partisan of Mark Antony, suffect consul in 40 BCE.
Publius Carisius was a Roman general under Augustus, legate in Hispania Ulterior during the Cantabrian Wars.
Ambiorix was a king of the Eburones, a Belgic people between the Meuse and the Rhine, who ruled jointly with Catuvolcus.
Diviciacus was a druid and leading noble of the Aedui of central Gaul and the only druid known by name from antiquity.
Dubnovellaunus was a British king of the late 1st century BCE and early 1st century CE known from coins issued in Kent and among the Trinovantes of Essex.
Dumnacus was a leader of the Andecavi, a Gallic people of the lower Loire around Angers.
